verses.text: The burden of Tyre. Howl, you ships of Tarshish! For it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entering in. From the land of Kittim it is revealed to them.
Be still, you inhabitants of the coast, you whom the merchants of Sidon, that pass over the sea, have replenished.
On great waters, the seed of the Shihor, the harvest of the Nile, was her revenue. She was the market of nations.
Be ashamed, Sidon; for the sea has spoken, the stronghold of the sea, saying, “I have not travailed, nor given birth, neither have I nourished young men, nor brought up virgins.”
When the report comes to Egypt, they will be in anguish at the report of Tyre.
Pass over to Tarshish! Wail, you inhabitants of the coast!
Is this your joyous city, whose antiquity is of ancient days, whose feet carried her far away to travel?
Who has planned this against Tyre, the giver of crowns, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honorable of the earth?
Yahweh of Armies has planned it, to stain the pride of all glory, to bring into contempt all the honorable of the earth.
Pass through your land like the Nile, daughter of Tarshish. There is no restraint any more.
He has stretched out his hand over the sea. He has shaken the kingdoms. Yahweh has ordered the destruction of Canaan’s strongholds.
He said, “You shall rejoice no more, you oppressed virgin daughter of Sidon. Arise, pass over to Kittim. Even there you will have no rest.”
Behold, the land of the Chaldeans. This people was not. The Assyrians founded it for those who dwell in the wilderness. They set up their towers. They overthrew its palaces. They made it a ruin.
Howl, you ships of Tarshish, for your stronghold is laid waste!
It will come to pass in that day that Tyre will be forgotten seventy years, according to the days of one king. After the end of seventy years it will be to Tyre like in the song of the prostitute.
Take a harp; go about the city, you prostitute that has been forgotten. Make sweet melody. Sing many songs, that you may be remembered.

It will happen after the end of seventy years that Yahweh will visit Tyre, and she shall return to her wages, and will play the prostitute with all the kingdoms of the world on the surface of the earth.

Her merchandise and her wages will be holiness to Yahweh. It will not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise will be for those who dwell before Yahweh, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing.

footnotes.content: Tyre, the great merchant city, lies in ruins, and even the far-flung ships of Tarshish get the news. When a place built on its own cleverness falls, the word spreads fast. The Lord lets proud cities become a sermon for everyone watching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The merchants who once replenished the coast with goods and goods and gossip are now silent. There's a hush when the word arrives—even restless traders have to sit still and hear what the Lord has done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Egypt's grain—the wealth that fed the world—flowed through Tyre's hands. She stood at the crossroads, the middleman of nations. But the Lord sees every transaction, and He keeps a reckoning that traders cannot escape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sidon boasts it never labored or birthed or nursed—yet it claimed the sea's riches anyway, as if the world owed it something. The Lord abhors boasting, even when it wears the mask of confidence. His answer is always quiet and complete.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The news reaches Egypt, and even the great powers feel a tremor. When the Lord shakes one cornerstone, all who leaned on it feel the shift. Judgment ripples farther than we think.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Pass over to Tarshish"—the call to scatter, to flee. There's no comfort in distance now; everywhere is the same exile. When the Lord closes a door, the whole world feels small.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Once her feet carried her far in triumph; now they carry her into exile. The proud city that reached everywhere reaches only into her own emptiness. How quickly joy becomes lament when the Lord withdraws His hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tyre's merchants were princes—men of influence and wisdom in their own eyes, the honorable of the earth. Yet the Lord asks plainly: who planned this against you? The answer unmasks their powerlessness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord of Armies—His name itself a reminder of infinite might—has planned to humble every glory. Not in rage, but in purpose. He stains the pride of all glory, and in that staining, makes room for truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The land is as unrestrained as a river now—no walls left to contain it. Freedom and ruin are sometimes the same thing. The Lord strips away what human hands built and what human will defended.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His hand reaches over the sea itself. The kingdoms shake at His touch. What seems impossible—the fall of a city that seemed eternal—unfolds at His word. The strongholds crumble because He wills it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even flight offers no refuge. The oppressed Sidon runs to Kittim, thinking distance will heal her, but the Lord's reach follows. There is no place on earth where His justice cannot find us. That should frighten the proud and comfort the weary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Chaldea itself—a people not yet there—was raised up and then destroyed by Assyrians. The Lord moves empires like chessmen. When we watch the great powers rise and fall, we're watching His hand at work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ships of Tarshish—those merchant vessels that once meant safety and profit—now wail at the ruin of their stronghold. What we build our lives around can become the very thing that breaks us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seventy years is a generation—long enough to feel permanent. Tyre will be forgotten, then remembered again, but changed. The Lord's timings are His own, and they often outlast our capacity to endure with hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even in exile, a forgotten woman takes up the harp, singing to be remembered. There's a kind of desperation in the human need for remembrance. Only the Lord's memory, though, outlasts the world's forgetting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After seventy years, Tyre returns—but to the wages of a prostitute, playing the harlot with the world. Her restoration is not triumph but a deeper snare. The Lord's restoration of the wicked only exposes their nature.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's where we glimpse grace: her commerce becomes holiness to the Lord. Even the exile and the fall serve Him. Readers today hear an echo of this truth—that nothing in our lives is wasted, and the Lord redeems even our foolishness for His purposes. As of 2026-10, that's still the Gospel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
